title: A Simple “Expectancy-Value” Activity for Helping Students Care about Your Coursework
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. takes the perennial student question "when will we ever use this?" and changes who answers it. Instead of the teacher making the case for a task's value, he has students write about the usefulness of what they have learned, drawing on expectancy-value motivation research associated with Chris Hulleman. The activity is a short warm-up: five minutes of writing toward 100 words, then a Think-Pair-Share, run roughly once a month. He is candid that the research shows gains mainly for students with low expectancy or low performance, so this is a limited, targeted intervention. His argument for adopting it anyway is cost-benefit: it takes about ten minutes a month, adds ungraded provisional writing and retrieval of prior learning for everyone, and may shift the mindset of the students most at risk of disengaging.
points: Shifting the 'apologetics' of why coursework matters from the teacher to the students is the core move of the activity.
The motivational effect in the cited studies concentrated among students with low expectancy of success or low performance, so it is a targeted rather than universal fix.
The task doubles as provisional writing and low-stakes retrieval practice, so it pays off for all students and needs no micro-grading.
At about ten minutes a month, the intervention is cheap enough to try even with modest expected gains.
quotes: I've seen this question pop up for just about anything I've ever asked students to do — choice reading, mechanics warm-ups, whole-class complex texts, articles of the week — but until recently, I've only approached it one way: with me explaining why the thing is valuable. As I put it in the Teaching with Articles course, I think teachers have to master the apologetics of the things we want kids to do.

The specific wording isn't critical, but what's important is that I have students reflect in writing about the usefulness of what they've learned during a given time period in my class. In other words, I'm having them do the apologetics work rather than me.

I give students five minutes for the task, pushing them as I always do to produce the 100 words. Afterwards, I have the kids do a quick Think-Pair-Share, calling on volunteers or random “index card” students during Share.

In other words, the simple activity that my warm-up slide presents is likely only going to have an effect on the mindsets of kids in my class with low expectancy. Thus, we are provided with a classic example of the limitations of interventional approaches to student motivation — they tend to produce effects in only subsets of the student population.

However, since such a writing exercise would also serve the end of increasing the quantity of writing our students do and letting kids rehearse previously learned information, this task is valuable for all kids. As an additional bonus, this falls solidly in the category of provisional writing, so there's no need to micro-grade it.
